newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Ukraine's varied city Chernivtsi falling to pieces.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ukraine's varied city Chernivtsi falling to pieces.

text.p: Perched on a hillside and passed back and forth for centuries between competing masters, the city of Chernivtsi in western Ukraine is falling apart.
What is not tumbling into post-Soviet disrepair may fall instead into the surrounding ravines because years of neglect have left the town prey to devastating landslides.
Chernivtsi, centre of northern Bucovina, has been a beacon of learning, enterprise and the arts for Ukrainians, Russians, Romanians, Germans and Jews.
"Some traditions have maintained their hold here, thank goodness. Soviet rule left its mark but not a big one," said Taras Kiyak, a member of parliament for the city of 280,000.
"You can see it in the way people mix. There was never any trouble between different groups. And our past made reforms easier. People understood private property. It's in the blood."
An eastern outpost of the Austro-Hungarian empire last century, it fell under Romanian control after World War One.
The Nazi-Soviet pact carving up eastern Europe handed it to the Kremlin in 1940 only to have it bounce back to Romania a year later when their German allies pushed through the region.
The Red Army's counter-offensive placed the city back in Soviet hands and it reverted to independent Ukraine with the fall of communism in 1991.
ARCHITECTURE REFLECTS CITY'S PAST
Every street in the old city centre bears the architectural traces of whoever was in charge, for however short a time.

The grandiose railway station reflects 19th century rule under emperor Franz Josef as does a magnificent university which once housed senior Orthodox clerics. Mosaics on painted Austrian houses blend with Romanian cupola roofs and square, modernist buildings erected between the world wars.
On the outskirts -- the endless crumbling tower blocks that blight most ex-Soviet cities.
POST-SOVIET DECLINE MARKS CITY

Chernivtsi is reeling from the decline gripping post-Soviet Ukraine. Factories lining the Prut river -- built in the mid-1960s after the Soviet leadership became sure Romania would not demand the return of the region -- virtually all stand idle, windows broken, machinery rusting in courtyards.
Painted houses and ornate hotel facades in the centre cry out for a coat of paint. The open-air theatre in the city's largest park is out of action since its roof fell in.
"I was in shock when I saw the state of the buildings we put up 30 years ago," said Natan Shufer, 55, returning to Chernivtsi for the first time since he left for Israel in 1973.

"There's no money -- to renovate buildings, to keep the cobbled streets in shape. And my friends, graduates like me, some had so little to live on they hadn't eaten for a week. One was just glad to have a chicken in the yard to keep him fed."
Poverty has dulled the memories of people old enough to remember life under pre-Soviet rulers.
"My grandfather was Czech. He married my Polish mother here when it was Austrian," said Kateryna, one of a clutch of kerchiefed women outside the Polish Roman Catholic church.
Her monthly pension, equivalent to $25, just covered the rent when topped up with an additional government benefit.
"What difference does it make whether it was better back then?" she said. "I know that now my relatives in Poland live better and even have enough to help their children."
A MULTI-ETHNIC POPULATION

Local officials deflect charges in Bucharest that Ukraine is assimilating Bucovina's 200,000-strong Romanian minority, most of whom live in villages near Chernivtsi. They point to dozens of schools, seven newspapers and daily broadcasts in Romanian.

"I was born in Siberia. The same people who sent my family there (Russian communists) sent off plenty of Romanians too," said Petro Hasyuk, deputy chairman of the regional council. "No ethnic minority in Europe has such advantages."

Of 100,000 Jews at the turn of the century, less than one-tenth remain. Chernivtsi was a staging point for the 1970s departure of Soviet Jews to Israel through Romania -- the only communist country to maintain ties then with the Jewish state.

Residents recall five synagogues in the city. In the mid-1950s local communist party bosses ordered the largest to be blown up, but repeated attempts to level it failed and it was left to operate as the "October" cinema.
LANDSLIDES
But the most deadly threat may come from the landslides.

"The slides are caused by bad drainage. Between 30 and 60 percent of the city's water goes straight into the ground," said Zinovy Broide, a conservation specialist, who champions a project of joint water management with Romania.
"The Austrians designed the drainage system and when their engineers left no one really knew how it worked," Broide said outside a hospital abandoned since the last big slide in 1995.
"It decayed under Romania and was only patched up in Soviet times. If we don't find a solution, we could have a disaster."
HOME TO MUSICIANS AND ARTISTS
Chernivtsi nonetheless has a versatility rare in ex-Soviet cities, particularly in musical and literary traditions.

A symphony orchestra was created two years ago by graduates of the local music school. That was a rare achievement in a country where state subsidies have dried up and cultural figures are reduced to going abroad to escape paltry salaries.

"The people in Bucovina were always a musical people," said Valentyna Diyakovska of the Ukrainian Culture Fund, who runs an arts and craft shop to promote young musicians and help "veterans of culture" destitute at the end of their careers.
"The arts thrived here under Austria and Romania too. In Soviet times, so many of the country's intellectuals came from here. People would go away to study but always come back."
But even versatility has its limits as young educated people find it difficult to make their way.

"This is indeed a wonderful place, but once my job finishes what am I do to here?" said Irina, a fluent French speaker whose job with a Western project ends in the summer. "I'll have to go somewhere. There's no future for me here."
